title: Exposure to untrustworthy websites in the 2020 US election
screen_reason: Behavioural panel study: 7.5 million URL-level website visits passively logged from 1,151 US adults (YouGov Pulse) around the 2020 election, matched against a list of 1,796 untrustworthy domains. It reports the share of Americans exposed to at least one untrustworthy website (26.2%), which is a REACH estimate with a stated denominator, plus per-person exposure intensity and party subgroup shares. Meets the REACH/EXPOSURE inclusion criterion.

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop, laptop and mobile browsers), YouGov Pulse plugin
estimates.measure_type: % of American adults who visited at least one untrustworthy website during the 2020 election period
estimates.denominator: 1,151 American adults with passively tracked web browsing (YouGov Pulse panel, weighted to approximate US population demographics), 7.5 million website visits
estimates.definition: Respondent visited, at least once during the tracking window, any of 1,796 web domains classified as untrustworthy (domains rated by NewsGuard as repeatedly publishing false content, plus the Guess et al. and Allcott et al. untrustworthy-domain lists). Domain-level, not article-level.
estimates.misinfo_def: "untrustworthy websites were considered web domains that NewsGuard rated as repeatedly hosting false information (or imported from the database used by Guess et al.)"; the Guess et al. list consisted of domains that "frequently publish factually dubious or untrustworthy content"
estimates.source_quote: By contrast, we find that during the 2020 election, only 26.2% (95% CI 22.5% to 29.8%) of Americans were exposed to at least one untrustworthy website.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Total consumption of untrustworthy websites in 2020'; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: List of 1,796 unique untrustworthy domains: 490 from Guess, Nyhan & Reifler (2020), 66 more from Allcott, Gentzkow & Yu (2019), and 1,240 domains rated by NewsGuard (an organisation of former journalists and news editors who manually rate website information quality, database updated weekly) as 'repeatedly publishing false content'. No inter-coder reliability reported; ratings are proprietary to NewsGuard.
estimates.moderator_quote: We added the 1,240 domains that NewsGuard rated as 'repeatedly publishing false content' to the Guess et al. and Allcott et al. list of untrustworthy websites, producing a total list of 1,796 unique untrustworthy domains. [...] untrustworthy websites were operationalized at the domain level.
estimates.notes: Headline estimate of the paper and the row to pool. Weighted to the US adult population. topic coded politics_elections because the data window, framing and predictors are electoral, but note the domain list itself is NOT topic-restricted (NewsGuard flags sites that repeatedly publish false content on any subject), so general_news is a defensible alternative coding. Measurement floor: browser-only (no in-app activity), mobile data available for just 30.1% of participants, and domain-level matching misses misinformation on otherwise-reliable domains and content viewed inside dynamic URLs (e.g. a Facebook feed).

estimates.platform: Web browsing (desktop, laptop and mobile browsers), YouGov Pulse plugin

estimates.source_quote: First, the average number of untrustworthy website visits among those who visited at least one untrustworthy website in 2020 (22.8 visits; 95% CI 15.2 to 30.4) was significantly lower than the average number in 2016 (32.1 visits; 95% CI 26.3 to 37.9)
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Total consumption of untrustworthy websites in 2020'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 1,796-domain list (Guess et al. 490 + Allcott et al. 66 + NewsGuard 1,240 'repeatedly publishing false content').
estimates.moderator_quote: the average number of untrustworthy website visits among those who visited at least one untrustworthy website in 2020 (22.8 visits; 95% CI 15.2 to 30.4)
estimates.notes: Not a percentage: a per-capita count of visits, CONDITIONAL on being exposed at least once (denominator is the exposed 26.2%, not the whole sample). Keep out of any pooled prevalence share.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) EVERY 2016 figure in this paper (44.3% exposed; 32.1 visits; 64.2 s; 59.5% of Trump and 37.1% of Clinton supporters; 85.2% of the most conservative decile; 56.2% of those 65+; 25.3% visiting a fact-checking site; 15.1% Facebook / 3.3% Google / 9.5% webmail referrals) is taken from Guess, Nyhan & Reifler (2020) or recomputed from their replication data. R8 forbids keeping a figure the paper cites from elsewhere, so none of them is extracted here; they should come from the Guess et al. record instead. (2) Other 2020 subgroup shares NOT given rows, to avoid burying the headline: 37.4% (95% CI 29.6-45.2) of people 65 years and older exposed; exposure by device, 34.2% (95% CI 29.4-39.1) on desktop/laptop vs 13% (95% CI 8.9-17.2) on smartphones and tablets; the media-slant decile estimates in Fig. 1 (Supplementary Table 7, values not in the text). An adjudicator who wants age as a moderator can add the 65+ row from the verbatim sentence 'only 37.4% (95% CI 29.6% to 45.2%) of people 65 years and older were exposed in 2020'. (3) Average time on untrustworthy sites in 2020 (38.6 s; 95% CI 34.5 to 42.7) is a duration, not a share or a per-capita count of items, so no row. (4) Referrer shares (5.6% of visits to untrustworthy sites referred by Facebook, 6.2% by Google, 5.7% by webmail in 2020) are computed inside the untrustworthy-visit set and their numerator is the referring platform, not falsity, so they are not prevalence estimates. (5) 13.1% (95% CI 11.2-15.2) of Americans visited a FACT-CHECKING site in 2020 - exposure to fact checks, not to misinformation, so out of scope. (6) 'nearly 68 million Americans made a total of 1.5 billion visits to untrustworthy sites' is a population extrapolation, not a share. (7) The paper reports no diet-share ('% of all browsing that was untrustworthy') in the main text; any such figure would be in the Supplementary Materials, which are not in this file. (8) The intro cites Grinberg et al.'s 1%-of-users/80%-of-fake-news concentration finding, but it is another study's number, so no CONCENTRATION row.

rob.design: Passive URL-level web-browsing data (desktop, laptop and mobile browsers) collected with the YouGov Pulse plugin from 1,151 consenting US adults, 2 Oct - 9 Nov 2020, yielding 7.5 million website visits, paired with an online survey; YouGov weighted participants to approximate US population demographics and the weights are used throughout. Untrustworthy exposure defined at the DOMAIN level against a 1,796-domain list (490 Guess et al. + 66 Allcott et al. + 1,240 NewsGuard 'repeatedly publishes false content'); no per-article coding and hence no inter-coder reliability. Design deliberately mirrors Guess, Nyhan & Reifler (2020) for comparability, with two changes: a list over three times larger, and inclusion of mobile browsing (available for only 30.1% of participants). No response/attrition rate reported. Acknowledged limitations: in-app use invisible, dynamic-URL content (feeds) invisible, misinformation on otherwise-reliable domains invisible. Stanford IRB protocol 53941; data and code on OSF, full traffic histories withheld.
rob.item6_quote: That is, in our data, untrustworthy websites were considered web domains that NewsGuard rated as repeatedly hosting false information (or imported from the database used by Guess et al.) (for example, www.obamawatcher.com), rather than specific web pages or articles.
rob.item10_quote: By contrast, we find that during the 2020 election, only 26.2% (95% CI 22.5% to 29.8%) of Americans were exposed to at least one untrustworthy website.
